title: Customer Survey

jokes.text: "Nothing can hurt you now. You're a man in love!"
jokes.setup: Michael is congratulating someone on an engagement that is not real
jokes.punchline: The grandiose romantic proclamation lands hollow because the premise is entirely false
jokes.explanation: Michael's delusion layered onto romantic idealism is a reliable character note. Mildly funny but derivative of the broader Michael-is-oblivious setup.

jokes.text: "I was there. That dude is not engaged. I'm not a big believer in therapy, but... I'll go into my own pockets to cover his co-pay."
jokes.setup: Dwight establishes the engagement is fake, then pivots to concern for Michael's mental state
jokes.punchline: Dwight's offer to fund Michael's therapy co-pay out of his own pocket — both deadpan and revealing Dwight's twisted loyalty
jokes.explanation: This is an elegant Dwight joke — he dismisses therapy in principle but would personally fund it for Michael. The self-contradiction is character-specific and delivered with total sincerity. Good economy, good character integration.

jokes.text: "Big idea: double wedding. Me, Angela. You, Holly. We would never do that. And if we did, it would be with Jim and Pam."
jokes.setup: Michael floats a double wedding idea
jokes.punchline: Dwight immediately shuts it down, then specifies the CORRECT double wedding partners — treating Jim and Pam as the default superior option over Holly
jokes.explanation: The funny layer is Dwight's Schrute-logic hierarchy of double wedding eligibility. He doesn't say 'no double weddings' — he says 'not with Holly.' That specificity is what makes it work.

jokes.text: "Michael, I got my bridesmaid dress. And you said I could get it in any color I wanted, so I picked white."
jokes.setup: Phyllis announces she already got her bridesmaid dress for Michael's non-existent wedding
jokes.punchline: She chose white — the bride's color — which is both socially wrong and hilariously passive-aggressive from Phyllis
jokes.explanation: A beautifully compressed joke: Phyllis bought a dress for a fake wedding AND chose the bride's color. The setup ('you said any color') makes her seem compliant before the punchline reveals she picked the most loaded color possible. Very economical. Phyllis's deadpan delivery implies she either doesn't know or absolutely knows — both readings are funny. Strong craft.

jokes.text: "Whenever I'm getting married, you... don't believe me."
jokes.setup: Mom says 'No, you're not' to Michael's engagement announcement
jokes.punchline: Michael's wounded complaint implies this has happened so many times it's become a pattern — 'whenever I'm getting married'
jokes.explanation: The phrase 'whenever I'm getting married' is the gem — it implies a recurring cycle of fake engagements so casually that Michael doesn't notice he's indicting himself. Perfect character comedy. Could only be Michael Scott. The mom's skepticism is fully earned and the line retroactively deepens our understanding of him.

jokes.text: Michael admits 'I'm not. I'm not getting married.' — long beat of humiliation
jokes.setup: Michael is caught — mom didn't believe him, and he has to concede in front of the whole office
jokes.punchline: The deflated, quiet 'I'm not. I'm not getting married.' after all the enthusiasm is the comedic and emotional crash
jokes.explanation: The cringe payoff of the phone call sequence. Steve Carell's delivery of dejected admission is the laugh — it's a performance joke more than a writing joke. The repeated 'I'm not' suggests he's processing the reality.

jokes.text: 'Psych.'
jokes.setup: Michael has just quietly admitted he's not getting married, apparently ending the humiliating scene
jokes.punchline: After a long beat, Michael says 'Psych' — trying to reframe the entire confession as a prank, which fools no one
jokes.explanation: The single word 'Psych' after an extended moment of genuine emotional exposure is a perfect Office button. It's pathetic and funny simultaneously — Michael trying to save face with a middle-school deflection. The economy score is a 10 because one word does enormous comedic work. Highly quotable and rewatchable.

jokes.text: "So, I returned my bridesmaid dress, and it was on sale, so I'm out $100. And I'm out a fiancee."
jokes.setup: Phyllis reports the aftermath of the fake engagement — she returned her white bridesmaid dress
jokes.punchline: Michael's 'And I'm out a fiancee' — treating an imaginary engagement loss as equivalent to Phyllis's real $100 loss
jokes.explanation: The parallel structure of 'I'm out $100 / I'm out a fiancee' is clean and funny. Phyllis has a concrete loss; Michael's loss is entirely fictional. The equivalence he draws is both sad and absurd.

jokes.text: "Kelly Kapoor is our dusky, exotic, customer service rep... Sort of a Kapoor's list. Schindler's List parody."
jokes.setup: Michael introduces Kelly professionally during a talking head
jokes.punchline: He calls her 'dusky, exotic' (racist), then compares the customer survey list to Schindler's List — and immediately explains the reference as if the camera doesn't know
jokes.explanation: Two-layer joke: the casual racism of 'dusky, exotic' is pure Michael obliviousness, and then 'Kapoor's List / Schindler's List parody' — he explains his own joke to the camera, which is a great character beat (Michael always over-explains). The Schindler's List reference is tonally wild which is the point. Slightly bloated by the explanation.

jokes.text: "Which is kind of great for me because, you wouldn't know from looking at her, but... Pam's a gold digger. New York ain't free. Get back to work."
jokes.setup: Jim explains that the customer survey scores affect bonuses
jokes.punchline: Jim calls Pam a 'gold digger' — a loving, self-deprecating joke about their finances — then snaps 'New York ain't free. Get back to work.' at the camera
jokes.explanation: 'You wouldn't know from looking at her' is a misdirect — suggesting something negative about Pam, then 'gold digger' as the punchline reframes it affectionately. 'New York ain't free' then snaps the camera back. The talking-head pivot is a nice structural move.

jokes.text: Jim and Pam reveal they're secretly connected via the world's tiniest Bluetooth earpiece all day — talking to each other during the workday without anyone knowing
jokes.setup: Jim holds up a tiny Bluetooth earpiece, explains he found it in a Japanese gadget store and got one for Pam in New York
jokes.punchline: They've been talking all day secretly — the company has an 8-hour personal call policy so they're just not telling anyone
jokes.explanation: The Bluetooth premise is a season-five romantic device that's also genuinely clever as a comedic setup — it creates opportunities for Pam to comment on Scranton events remotely and Jim to seem bizarre to coworkers. The 'company has a policy against 8-hour personal calls, so we're not telling anyone' is a great logical close. Strong character integration: only Jim and Pam's long-distance relationship generates this kind of creative workaround.

jokes.text: "Pam, what do you want in your coffee? Sprinkle of cinnamon."
jokes.setup: Jim is at the coffee station, speaking into his ear — to the office it looks like he's talking to himself
jokes.punchline: The mundane domesticity of asking about coffee flavoring is funny because it's happening secretly in a workplace setting via spy gadget
jokes.explanation: The cinnamon detail is the kind of small, specific, domestic intimacy that makes Jim and Pam's relationship feel real and funny simultaneously. It's sweet and absurd at once — using a spy gadget for 'sprinkle of cinnamon.'

jokes.text: "All righty, Dwighty, let's see how you did." / Dwight's survey results are terrible — he's described as 'abrasive and distasteful'
jokes.setup: Dwight is confident going into his customer survey review — 'Bring it on'
jokes.punchline: Michael's face falls — 'No... Sorry.' — the scores are terrible
jokes.explanation: Standard Dwight-is-oblivious-about-his-social-skills joke. The 'All righty, Dwighty' rhyme from Michael is a nice small touch. Functional but not exceptional.

jokes.text: "Wait, is this a joke? I'm getting that queasy feeling that sometimes accompanies jokes."
jokes.setup: Dwight hears his terrible survey results and can't believe they're real
jokes.punchline: Dwight describes his physical response to jokes — 'that queasy feeling that sometimes accompanies jokes' — as if jokes are a diagnosable medical condition he monitors
jokes.explanation: This is exceptional Dwight writing. The line 'the queasy feeling that sometimes accompanies jokes' is brilliant character comedy — Dwight has catalogued his own biological response to humor as a clinical symptom rather than laughter. It suggests he's been in situations where he couldn't tell if someone was joking and learned to identify it via nausea. The follow-up exchange ('Do I look like I'm joking?' / 'No, but that's sometimes part of it') escalates it perfectly. This could only be Dwight. High originality, perfect economy, fully earned.

jokes.text: "If I were joking, you'd be laughing. Do you look like you are laughing?" / "Impossible to say. I can't see myself."
jokes.setup: Michael tries to convince Dwight the bad scores are real by saying 'I'm not joking'
jokes.punchline: Dwight's literal response — 'Impossible to say. I can't see myself.' — is the perfect absurdist Dwight non-sequitur
jokes.explanation: Pure Dwight logic: Michael asks 'Do you look like you're laughing?' as a rhetorical device, but Dwight takes it literally — he literally cannot see his own face to confirm. The joke is that Dwight has an unassailable point by the most absurd logic possible. Perfectly structured and character-specific. A companion to the queasy joke above.

jokes.text: Andy barges in to gloat about his good scores, calls Jim 'Tommy Tuna', uses Jim's mug without asking
jokes.setup: Andy cheerfully intrudes on a tense conversation to celebrate his own good scores
jokes.punchline: 'Tommy Tuna' as a nickname for Jim — confident, unprompted, slightly unhinged
jokes.explanation: Andy's social obliviousness (barging in when clearly unwanted) is reliable character comedy. 'Tommy Tuna' is a funny non-sequitur nickname. The mug conflict that develops is the bigger joke.

jokes.text: The mug standoff: Andy drinks from Jim's mug (which has Jim's face on it), won't give it back, Jim says 'It has my face on it' / Andy: 'Make the face.'
jokes.setup: Andy picked up Jim's mug and won't acknowledge it's Jim's — even when Jim points out the mug has his face on it
jokes.punchline: 'Make the face' — Andy demands Jim replicate his mug-photo expression to prove ownership
jokes.explanation: 'Make the face' is a perfect escalation of an absurd dispute. Andy demands Jim prove the mug is his by replicating the photo — turning a simple 'that's my mug' argument into a face-matching challenge. The escalation logic is airtight and the punchline lands hard. Quotable, very Andy.

jokes.text: Jim describes Dwight's emotional noise to Pam: "That was Dwight. He seems upset about something. Describe him exactly. What color mustard is his shirt? Yellow or Dijon?" — "It is more of a spicy brown, actually."
jokes.setup: Jim hears Dwight upset and narrates to Pam via Bluetooth; Pam asks for a description
jokes.punchline: The mustard color taxonomy (yellow vs. Dijon vs. 'spicy brown') — Pam's correction of 'spicy brown' as a distinct mustard category is the absurdist punchline
jokes.explanation: This joke fires on multiple levels: Pam's remote participation in Scranton life via Bluetooth is romantic and funny; the mustard taxonomy (yellow, Dijon, spicy brown) as a Dwight-shirt classification system is absurdly specific; and 'spicy brown' as Pam's correction is the perfect escalating punchline. The whole exchange is warm and clever. Strong character integration — Pam still knows Dwight's wardrobe from New York.

jokes.text: Dwight says he's 'being sabotaged' about his bad scores; Jim's response: 'Or you could just be nice to your customers.' Dwight: 'You're an idiot.' Jim: 'There's the charm.'
jokes.setup: Dwight insists he's being sabotaged and will punish whoever is responsible
jokes.punchline: Jim's sensible suggestion ('be nice to your customers') is met with 'You're an idiot' — Jim's 'There's the charm' immediately underlines the irony
jokes.explanation: 'There's the charm' is a clean, economical callback-within-the-moment — Jim watching Dwight demonstrate the exact problem being discussed. Perfect straight-man beat.

jokes.text: Jim says 'Love you' into the Bluetooth; Andy/Dwight stare confused as Jim apparently talks to himself; Dwight: 'What do you think I am saying to you?' Jim: 'Not talking to you.'
jokes.setup: Jim says 'Love you' and 'Thanks' into his earpiece to Pam mid-conversation
jokes.punchline: From everyone else's perspective, Jim is talking to himself — Dwight's bewildered 'What do you think I am saying to you?' is a perfect confused straight-man beat
jokes.explanation: Solid execution of the Bluetooth premise — Jim's tenderness toward Pam looks like madness to everyone else. Dwight's response plays perfectly as both confused and offended.

jokes.text: "I've caught Jim talking to himself several times today. What a loser. Get a friend, loser!"
jokes.setup: Dwight has observed Jim apparently talking to himself all day via the Bluetooth
jokes.punchline: Dwight's talking-head: 'What a loser. Get a friend, loser!' — not knowing Jim is talking to Pam
jokes.explanation: The dramatic irony is the engine — we know Jim is talking to Pam, Dwight thinks he's a friendless lunatic. 'Get a friend, loser!' is a funny talking-head button. The double irony that Jim absolutely has a friend (his fiancée) makes it even better.

jokes.text: Michael on phone describing the 'Shangri-La tent' wedding — 'It's two stories, heated, and it has a bridal suite for my bridal sweet.'
jokes.setup: Michael describes his elaborate wedding tent plans
jokes.punchline: 'Bridal sweet' — a malapropism for 'bridal suite,' but also accidentally a pun (sweet = term of endearment), which Michael is completely unaware of
jokes.explanation: 'Bridal sweet' is a Michael malapropism that works as an accidental pun — Michael would use the wrong word ('sweet' instead of 'suite') and the writers made it a double entendre. Character-appropriate and nicely compressed.

jokes.text: "I found the best 'tentist' on the east coast. He personally tented Giuliani's first and third weddings. And I got him!"
jokes.setup: Michael describes his wedding tent vendor with increasing excitement
jokes.punchline: 'Tentist' as a made-up professional title — Michael invents the word for a tent specialist; 'Giuliani's first AND third weddings' implies skipping the second (a dark joke about Giuliani's marriages)
jokes.explanation: Two jokes in one sentence: 'tentist' as Michael's invented word (like 'conversationalist' but for tents) is funny in itself. Then 'first and third weddings' — the obvious implication is the second Giuliani wedding was so bad this tentist wasn't associated with it. The omission does the work. Both are economical and character-appropriate.

jokes.text: Michael tells Jim his scores are 'a poopy.'
jokes.setup: Jim finds out his customer survey scores are bad
jokes.punchline: 'They are a poopy' — Michael's infantile vocabulary to describe professional failure
jokes.explanation: 'A poopy' is a perfectly Michael word choice — childish, casual, used in a professional context. The brevity is the joke. It's a reliable Michael character beat.

jokes.text: "Jim Halpert is smudge and arrogant." Jim: "I think you mean 'smug'." Michael: "Arrogance. And there's our smudgeness."
jokes.setup: Michael reads aloud from Jim's terrible customer feedback
jokes.punchline: Michael mispronounces 'smug' as 'smudge,' Jim corrects him, and Michael uses Jim's correction as evidence of the very arrogance being criticized — 'And there's our smudgeness'
jokes.explanation: This is outstanding joke construction. Michael misreads 'smug' as 'smudge.' Jim corrects him — which is completely natural. Michael then weaponizes the correction as proof of Jim's arrogance ('there's our smudgeness'), while still using the wrong word. The joke works on three levels: Michael's misreading, Jim's reasonable correction becoming a trap, and Michael's self-satisfaction at catching Jim being 'smudge.' The structure is airtight. The persistence of 'smudgeness' (not even 'smugness') as the final word is the perfect cap. Exceptional.

jokes.text: "And if history tells us anything, it's that you can't go wrong buying a house you can't afford."
jokes.setup: Jim explains he needs a good bonus because he's secretly buying his parents' house for their retirement
jokes.punchline: The darkly ironic 'history tells us you can't go wrong buying a house you can't afford' — a reference to the 2008 housing crisis, delivered casually
jokes.explanation: This line is Season 5, 2008 — the housing crisis is happening in real time. Jim's deadpan ironic coda is sharp and topical. 'If history tells us anything' as a framing device before a line that inverts historical lesson is well-crafted. Slightly less character-specific (could be said by a few characters) but very well-executed.

jokes.text: "Pam doesn't know about the house, so... Fun surprise."
jokes.setup: Jim has secretly committed to buying his parents' house without telling Pam
jokes.punchline: 'Fun surprise.' — delivered as dry deadpan acknowledgment that this is absolutely not a fun surprise but a potentially disastrous financial secret
jokes.explanation: Two words doing enormous work. 'Fun surprise' implies Jim knows this is a potentially terrible idea but is committed to the delusion that it'll be fine. The economy is near-perfect. The camera look (implied) sells it.

jokes.text: Pam via Bluetooth: "Maybe it's cause you spent the whole year flirting with the receptionist." Jim: "A little bit. Worth it."
jokes.setup: Jim wonders why his scores might be bad
jokes.punchline: Pam calls herself 'the receptionist' — self-deprecating and teasing — and Jim's 'Worth it' confirms it completely, no defensiveness
jokes.explanation: Pam's self-referential 'the receptionist' acknowledges the entire Season 1-2 Jim/Pam dynamic in three words. Jim's 'Worth it' is the perfect, unambiguous reply. Beautiful economy. The joke rewards long-time viewers who know the history. Strong character integration.

jokes.text: "Here's what's going to happen. I am going to have to fix you... Manage you two on a more personal scale. A more micro form of management. Jim, what is that called?" Jim: "Microgement."
jokes.setup: Michael announces he's going to micromanage Jim and Dwight
jokes.punchline: Michael asks Jim to name the management style — 'micromanagement' — and Jim, playing along, says 'Microgement' (dropping 'manage')
jokes.explanation: The joke is Michael building to a word he doesn't know ('micromanagement') and Jim shortcutting it to a portmanteau. Mildly clever but not sharp. The setup is over-telegraphed.

jokes.text: The 'Buttlicker' cold call role-play: Dwight calls Jim (playing 'Bill Buttlicker') and takes the name seriously
jokes.setup: Michael sets up a role-play exercise where Dwight practices a customer call and Jim plays the client
jokes.punchline: Jim gives the name 'Bill Buttlicker' — Dwight almost laughs but holds it together when Michael warns him to be 'respectful'
jokes.explanation: The Buttlicker name is juvenile but the joke is in Dwight's struggle to maintain professionalism — and Michael coaching Dwight to 'be respectful' of a name that is inherently disrespectful. The premise builds to larger escalation.

jokes.text: "Really? That's your real name?" / "How dare you? My family built this country, by the way!"
jokes.setup: Dwight can't help questioning the name 'Buttlicker' despite Michael's warning to be respectful
jokes.punchline: Jim's 'Bill Buttlicker' counter-attacks with wounded pride — 'My family built this country' — delivered with complete sincerity
jokes.explanation: 'My family built this country, by the way' — Jim fully committing to 'Bill Buttlicker' as a dignified American patriarch is the escalation that makes the scene. The 'by the way' casualness is perfect.

jokes.text: Jim (as Buttlicker) pretends to take another call, tells the fictional person 'I'm just on the phone with this stupid salesman... I'm probably gonna keep him on hold forever and not buy anything.'
jokes.setup: Jim as 'Buttlicker' puts Dwight on hold to take 'another call'
jokes.punchline: Jim narrates his Buttlicker strategy aloud to the fake caller — telling Dwight exactly what's happening to him as a form of psychological torture
jokes.explanation: Jim openly sabotages Dwight's sales call by narrating the hostile client strategy to the client. The cruelty is precisely calibrated — it's sadistic but consequence-free within the exercise. Michael then says 'It's up to you to change his mind,' which frames Jim's behavior as a teaching opportunity, deepening the absurdity.

jokes.text: The 'hard of hearing old man' escalation: Dwight is forced to yell 'BUTTLICKER, OUR PRICES HAVE NEVER BEEN LOWER!' at increasing volume
jokes.setup: Jim's 'Buttlicker' character claims to be hard of hearing and keeps demanding Dwight speak louder
jokes.punchline: Dwight screams 'BUTTLICKER, OUR PRICES HAVE NEVER BEEN LOWER!' at full volume — Michael immediately shuts it down: 'You NEVER yell at the client.'
jokes.explanation: This is the comedic peak of the Buttlicker sequence. The escalating volume demands create inevitable physical comedy — Dwight must shout the name 'Buttlicker' in a professional context. The word itself becomes funnier each time it's said louder. Michael's immediate 'STOP IT. You NEVER yell at the client' is the perfect straight-faced authority response to a completely absurd situation. The scene is expertly structured: Dwight is trapped between Michael's rules (be respectful) and Jim's manipulation (speak louder). Highly quotable, enormous room impact.

jokes.text: Dwight, scolded for yelling, pivots to: "The three words I would describe you as is aggressive, hostile, and definitely difficult." — echoing the exact language from his own bad reviews
jokes.setup: Dwight tries to recover after being told he can never yell at a client
jokes.punchline: Dwight describes 'Buttlicker' using exactly the words his own customers used to describe him — not realizing the irony
jokes.explanation: This is a structural callback — Michael read Dwight's reviews earlier ('abrasive and distasteful'), and now Dwight applies identical language to the fictional client. Dwight has zero self-awareness that he's describing himself. The callback is earned and the irony lands cleanly. Good construction.

jokes.text: Michael takes over the call as 'regional manager,' Buttlicker immediately loves him and pledges $1 million in paper: "I like the sound of your voice." Michael: "See how it's done?"
jokes.setup: Michael takes over the role-play to demonstrate how to handle a difficult client
jokes.punchline: Jim's 'Buttlicker' immediately caves and pledges $1 million — entirely because he 'likes the sound of Michael's voice' — Michael is smug about it
jokes.explanation: The joke is that Michael 'wins' the role-play because Jim lets him win (the scenario is fake), and Michael takes it as genuine proof of his salesmanship. Michael's smugness is funny but the sequence has slightly deflated at this point.

jokes.text: Buttlicker's condition: Michael must fire the salesman who treated him badly — 'Don't do it, Michael.' Michael considers it. 'It's a million-dollar sale.'
jokes.setup: The fictional $1 million sale comes with a condition: fire Dwight
jokes.punchline: Michael genuinely deliberates — 'It's a million-dollar sale' — suggesting he might actually fire Dwight for a fictional reason
jokes.explanation: The escalation of the role-play into genuine stakes (will Michael apply role-play consequences?) is a good concept but it gets left hanging rather than fully paid off.

jokes.text: Michael/Angela's wedding: 'I don't want to be married in a tent like a hobo.' Michael: 'Hobos live in trains.'
jokes.setup: Angela objects to the Shangri-La tent wedding venue
jokes.punchline: Michael corrects her hobo mythology — 'Hobos live in trains' — as if this is the important point to address
jokes.explanation: Michael's pedantic hobo correction ignores the actual complaint (she doesn't want a tent wedding) to address hobo housing. The specificity of 'Hobos live in trains' as a confident factual rebuttal is a solid Michael beat.

jokes.text: Holly: 'Nana Mimi can't be in canvas that long.'
jokes.setup: Holly is listing objections to the tent wedding
jokes.punchline: Introducing 'Nana Mimi' as a specific objection — the elderly relative who cannot tolerate canvas — is a funny, hyper-specific practical concern in an otherwise romantic discussion
jokes.explanation: A mild observational beat. The specificity of 'Nana Mimi' and 'canvas' is funny but the joke is fairly thin on its own.

jokes.text: Angela's wedding requirements: a hand-plowed field, an old barn where you can see stars through the roof slats when you lay on your back, and antique tools to look at when you roll over
jokes.setup: Angela agrees to a tent wedding — but only with specific conditions
jokes.punchline: The conditions escalate to increasingly specific pastoral requirements — 'antique tools to look at when you roll over' is the absurdist cap
jokes.explanation: Angela's wedding requirements are perfectly character-specific — she's austere, rural, Mennonite-adjacent, and utterly particular. The requirements escalate from plausible (field, barn) to very specific (see stars through roof slats) to absurdly specific (antique tools to look at when you roll over). The physical specificity of lying on your back, rolling over, and seeing tools implies Angela has done exactly this before. Vivid, weird, completely Angela.

jokes.text: Dwight drags Jim into his car to speak privately about sabotage — 'They might be listening to us.'
jokes.setup: Dwight believes there's a conspiracy behind his bad scores
jokes.punchline: He drags Jim into a car for a private meeting — then speculates the saboteurs could be 'the mob. Maybe NASA.'
jokes.explanation: Dwight's paranoia escalating to NASA as a potential saboteur of his paper sales scores is gloriously unhinged. The private car meeting as counter-surveillance theater is peak Dwight.

jokes.text: "Could be the mob. But then Dunder Mifflin would need to be a front for money laundering, and there's little evidence of that." Jim: "Is there some evidence?"
jokes.setup: Dwight theorizes the mob might be behind his bad reviews
jokes.punchline: Dwight dismisses the mob theory for lack of evidence — but the 'little evidence' qualifier implies there's SOME evidence Dunder Mifflin is mob-connected; Jim's 'Is there some evidence?' is the perfect straight-man follow
jokes.explanation: 'Little evidence' doing a lot of work — Dwight doesn't say 'no evidence,' he says 'little evidence,' which raises the implication that there might be some evidence of mob ties. Jim's immediate follow-up ('Is there some evidence?') is the perfect Jim reaction — he can't help engaging with the absurdity. Well-structured.

jokes.text: Dwight: 'Who stands to benefit from our downfall? The mob? Maybe NASA.'
jokes.setup: Dwight is listing possible saboteurs of his customer survey scores
jokes.punchline: The conspiratorial logic jumps from vaguely plausible (the mob) to completely unrelated (NASA) — delivered with total sincerity
jokes.explanation: The jump to NASA is perfectly timed absurdism. It's not random — Dwight has a logic (powerful organizations with resources), but the leap is so enormous it becomes brilliant. The flat delivery of 'Maybe NASA' after 'the mob' is excellent comedic economy.

jokes.text: Pam (via Bluetooth) is shopping for shoes online during Dwight's conspiracy rant; Jim: "How many shoes do you need?" — Dwight: "Who are you talking to?" Jim: "Pam." Dwight: "She's not here, Jim!"
jokes.setup: Dwight is laying out his paranoid conspiracy theory; Jim is simultaneously talking to Pam about shoes
jokes.punchline: The contrast of life-or-death conspiracy vs. shoe shopping, and Dwight's exasperation that Jim is talking to someone who 'isn't here'
jokes.explanation: The Bluetooth premise pays off again — Jim is half-present in Dwight's conspiracy meeting and half in a mundane shoe conversation with Pam. 'She's not here, Jim!' from Dwight is delivered with genuine concern that Jim may have lost his mind. Strong comedic contrast.

jokes.text: Michael announces the perfect wedding venue: 'A local bed and breakfast on a 60-acre beet farm... It's Dwight Schrute. As in Schrute Farms.'
jokes.setup: Michael has found the perfect rustic wedding venue — building anticipation for the reveal
jokes.punchline: It's Schrute Farms — Dwight's own property — which Michael has stumbled onto without connecting the obvious dots
jokes.explanation: The Schrute Farms reveal is a predictable beat for regular viewers but works as an earned setup for later Dwight wedding venue comedy. The 'As in Schrute Farms' explanation suggests Michael doesn't fully register the connection.

jokes.text: Dwight confronts Kelly in her 'nook' — a tiny customer service closet — and demands she admit to the conspiracy
jokes.setup: Dwight has found Kelly listening on the phone and suspects her of sabotage
jokes.punchline: Dwight invades her small private space (the 'nook') and calls her 'too stupid to do it by yourself'
jokes.explanation: The 'nook' as Kelly's personal territory that Dwight violates is a good physical setup for the scene, but the comedy here is mostly setup work for the 'That's what she said' payoff.

jokes.text: Dwight on the phone: 'Breathing. Is that you?' / 'Well, I am breathing, yes.' / 'Well, stop. Hold your breath.'
jokes.setup: Dwight suspects someone else is on the line during his sales call
jokes.punchline: His demand that the customer 'hold your breath' to eliminate interference is an absurd and dangerous request delivered as a perfectly reasonable security measure
jokes.explanation: Asking someone to stop breathing to eliminate audio interference is gloriously unhinged and completely Dwight. The customer's confused compliance ('Well, I am breathing, yes') makes it even better. Good economy.

jokes.text: Kelly: 'Dwight, get out of my nook!' Dwight: 'That's what she said! That's what she said!' — then immediately looks for validation
jokes.setup: Kelly tells Dwight to get out of her nook
jokes.punchline: Dwight deploys Michael's signature 'That's what she said' with enormous enthusiasm, repeating it twice — then clearly waiting for approval
jokes.explanation: The joke isn't 'That's what she said' per se — it's Dwight deploying it. Dwight never makes this joke. His saying it twice ('That's what she said! That's what she said!') and the implied desperate look for Michael's approval is what makes it land. The 'Good one.' response confirms it's Dwight reaching for the Michael-approved comedy tool. It's meta — we're laughing at Dwight doing a Michael impression. Strong character integration.

jokes.text: Jim tries to make small talk with Kelly — Kelly gives one-word answers and leaves. Jim: 'That was weird.' 'Have you ever had a conversation where she didn't go on for 15 minutes without taking a breath?'
jokes.setup: Jim talks to Kelly normally; she gives him the cold shoulder and exits in two words
jokes.punchline: Jim notes the absence of Kelly's signature verbal flood — her brevity is its own punchline because it's so out of character
jokes.explanation: The joke requires knowledge of Kelly's character — she is legendarily verbose. Her two-word exit ('We're cool. Bye.') is the comedic inversion. Jim's '15 minutes without taking a breath' is affectionate and accurate. Character-specific comedy that rewards viewer familiarity.

jokes.text: Ryan's talking head: 'I don't play the politics game anymore, Jim... I played it full-on in New York. I played it high stakes. For keeps. Made it to the top. But look what it costs.'
jokes.setup: Jim asks Ryan (now back as a temp after his corporate downfall) if Kelly might be mad at him
jokes.punchline: Ryan delivers this as profound wisdom — but 'making it to the top' and 'look what it costs' refers to him getting fired for fraud and returning as a temp. He still thinks he's impressive.
jokes.explanation: Ryan's grandiose self-mythology about his corporate 'rise' (he went to jail for fraud) delivered as hard-won wisdom to Jim is excellent character comedy. The gap between his self-perception and reality is the joke. 'Look what it costs' with him sitting in the bullpen as a temp is the unspoken punchline.

jokes.text: Jim asks Stanley if Kelly might be mad at him. Stanley: 'All right. Livin' in the moment. I don't play the politics game anymore, Jim. Can I tell you something? I played it full-on in New York. I played it high stakes. For keeps. Made it to the top.'
jokes.setup: Jim is trying to get information from Stanley about Kelly
jokes.punchline: Stanley pivots to an inexplicable monologue about his past life in New York politics — which is almost certainly fabricated or wildly exaggerated — delivered with deep, unearned gravitas
jokes.explanation: Stanley's sudden revelation of a secret high-stakes political past is wonderfully absurd and completely unexplained. 'Livin' in the moment' as his current philosophy contrasted with his supposed former life is a great character comedy beat. Stanley refusing to help while delivering this monologue is the joke.

jokes.text: Ryan mentions Kelly's America's Got Talent finale party — Jim didn't go. 'Crazy. It was packed. I thought everyone was there.' 'You were, remember you being there.' Jim: 'I wasn't, but thank you.'
jokes.setup: Ryan mentions a party Jim didn't attend — then claims Jim was there
jokes.punchline: Jim politely corrects Ryan, who has clearly just invented the memory. Jim's 'I wasn't, but thank you' is perfectly dry
jokes.explanation: 'I wasn't, but thank you' — Jim's acknowledgment that Ryan has simply invented his presence is characteristically dry. Ryan's confident false memory is a funny Ryan detail.

jokes.text: Via Bluetooth: 'I said you definitely should go, but you wanted to visit me instead.'
jokes.setup: Jim is learning he skipped Kelly's party to visit Pam in New York
jokes.punchline: Pam clarifies — confirming Jim chose her over the party — which is both sweet and the explanation for his professional consequences
jokes.explanation: A plot-clarifying beat that also serves as a callback to the 'Worth it' joke — Jim's choices consistently prioritize Pam over professional obligations. Functional but not especially crafted.

jokes.text: Jim tries to see Dwight's coffee mug (to confirm it's the Kelly party favor). Dwight hides it: 'No! Is that it? No. Why?'
jokes.setup: Jim suspects Dwight also skipped Kelly's party — and his mug would confirm it (Kelly gave them out as party favors)
jokes.punchline: Dwight immediately hides the mug and denies it — his guilty overreaction is funnier than the mug itself
jokes.explanation: The mug from the Andy subplot now returns as evidence in the Kelly conspiracy. The physical comedy of Dwight hiding it while denying everything is good. The callback to the earlier mug scene adds a layer.

jokes.text: Jim tells Dwight: 'I think it was Kelly... she's mad at us for not coming to her party.' Dwight: 'Man, I knew it. Who are her co-conspirators?' Jim: 'Probably just Kelly.' Dwight: 'Obviously. I knew it.'
jokes.setup: Jim explains the real (mundane) reason for their bad scores
jokes.punchline: Dwight immediately claims he 'knew it' — even though he was proposing NASA and the mob minutes ago; he retroactively owns Jim's conclusion as his own
jokes.explanation: Dwight's 'I knew it' after proposing NASA as a suspect is beautifully hypocritical. The rapid back-and-forth ('You were right. I was right. I knew it the whole time, buddy!') escalates into mutual congratulation that's slightly unhinged. Dwight's unselfconscious ownership of Jim's discovery is perfect character writing.

jokes.text: Jim and Dwight's mutual 'I knew it the whole time, buddy!' celebration — Dwight is so loud Michael hears from his office
jokes.setup: Jim and Dwight are doing mutual validation about having 'known' all along
jokes.punchline: The volume escalates until Michael hears — 'Right, Dwight is loud. I knew it!' — Dwight's final yell from offscreen is the button
jokes.explanation: The payoff of the celebration moment — Dwight's enthusiasm physically escaping the scene is a good button. 'Right, Dwight is loud' from Michael is a nice dry acknowledgment.

jokes.text: Michael confronts Kelly: 'Let me paint you a picture, of a little girl from southern India, who, despite being welcomed into this country, will now spend the rest of her life in prison for a crime she did commit.'
jokes.setup: Michael is about to confront Kelly about falsifying the survey results
jokes.punchline: 'A crime she did commit' — Michael undermines the usual innocence-presuming framing by confirming the crime upfront; also the 'welcomed into this country' is casual racism disguised as magnanimity
jokes.explanation: Michael's speech has the structure of a noble defense attorney's opening but immediately flips it — 'a crime she did commit' — with total obliviousness. 'Despite being welcomed into this country' is Michael being accidentally condescending while thinking he's being gracious. Strong Michael voice.

jokes.text: Michael to Kelly: 'Come on! You juked the stats, cupcake.'
jokes.setup: Michael is interrogating Kelly about falsifying the survey scores
jokes.punchline: 'You juked the stats, cupcake' — 'juked the stats' is The Wire slang used in a paper company context; 'cupcake' as a term of address undercuts any authority
jokes.explanation: 'You juked the stats, cupcake' is an exceptional line. 'Juked the stats' is directly from The Wire (a show about serious crime) applied to fake paper company customer surveys. 'Cupcake' as the term of address simultaneously undermines the toughness. The contrast between hard-boiled language and the actual stakes (customer surveys!) is perfectly compressed. High quotability, near-perfect economy.

jokes.text: Michael says he'll give Kelly one last chance. Kelly: 'I love your tie, Michael.'
jokes.setup: Michael is being stern, giving Kelly a final chance to confess
jokes.punchline: Kelly deploys a completely shameless, transparent compliment — 'I love your tie' — as a deflection, which is both obviously useless and perfectly Kelly
jokes.explanation: The non-sequitur compliment as a deflection is a great Kelly move — manipulative, transparent, and delivered with complete sincerity. 'I love your tie, Michael' is a perfect four-word punchline.

jokes.text: Kelly: 'I was raped.' Michael: 'You cannot say "I was raped" and expect all your problems to go away, Kelly. Not again. Don't keep doing that.'
jokes.setup: Kelly is cornered and about to confess to falsifying the surveys
jokes.punchline: 'Not again. Don't keep doing that.' — Michael's addendum implies Kelly has done this before as an escape hatch, treating it as a known Kelly deflection tactic
jokes.explanation: Dark joke that works through Michael's response more than Kelly's line — 'Not again. Don't keep doing that.' is the punchline, implying this is a recurring Kelly crisis-deflection move. Edgy, but the show earns it through character consistency. Scored slightly lower on 'earned vs. cheap' because the initial line is shock-value heavy.

jokes.text: Kelly: 'I was raped.' Michael: 'You cannot say I was raped and expect all your problems to go away, Kelly. Not again. Don't keep doing that.'
jokes.setup: Kelly is cornered and trying to escape accountability
jokes.punchline: 'Not again. Don't keep doing that' — Michael's exhausted, experienced correction implies Kelly has used this false accusation as a get-out-of-jail card before, which is both darkly funny and a devastating character note
jokes.explanation: This is a tonally risky joke that works because of 'Not again' — the implication of a prior pattern is what makes it funny rather than merely shocking. Michael's weary 'Don't keep doing that' transforms it from a one-off dark joke into a character revelation. The show earns this through Kelly's established dramatic tendencies.

jokes.text: Kelly confesses: 'I did it because you didn't come to my party, and you said you would try to, and then didn't even show up, and so you're bad friends.'
jokes.setup: Kelly has been caught falsifying professional customer surveys
jokes.punchline: The motive is entirely personal — not coming to her party makes them 'bad friends' — the disproportionate professional retaliation for a social slight is the joke
jokes.explanation: Kelly's confession is perfectly in character — she sabotaged colleagues' professional careers over a party. 'So you're bad friends' as the final moral indictment is exactly Kelly's worldview: professional life is subordinate to social life. The 'I did it, whatever. Just fire me.' is also great — she's more upset about the friendship betrayal than the work consequences. High character integration.

jokes.text: 'We have our confession. I'm calling security.' Dwight reaches for the phone — Michael stops him.
jokes.setup: Kelly has confessed; Dwight immediately escalates to maximum response
jokes.punchline: Dwight calling security for an office HR matter — treating a customer service dispute like a felony arrest
jokes.explanation: Consistent Dwight escalation. The 'we have our confession' phrasing is very Law & Order, which is the joke — Dwight treating a HR matter with procedural gravity.

jokes.text: After Kelly's confession: 'You know, she's got a point about you. You do have a problem dealing with people.' Dwight: 'See? I wasn't lying.' Michael: 'You were lying.' Dwight: 'I was lying.'
jokes.setup: Michael has just received Kelly's confession — she lied, but the underlying criticism has merit
jokes.punchline: Dwight's desperate need to be validated ('See? I wasn't lying') immediately capitulates when corrected ('You were lying' / 'I was lying') — total submission
jokes.explanation: The instant Dwight capitulation from 'I wasn't lying!' to 'I was lying' in two seconds when Michael says so is a perfect Dwight-Michael dynamic beat. Dwight's need for Michael's approval overrides his own self-defense.

jokes.text: Michael's talking head about always having too much leftover guacamole because people don't come to his parties: 'I can't tell you how much leftover guacamole I have ended up eating over the years. I don't even know why I make it in such great quantities.'
jokes.setup: Michael connects Kelly's party-snub pain to his own experience of people not showing up
jokes.punchline: The specificity of guacamole — made in 'great quantities' — and the resignation of eating it alone is both funny and genuinely sad
jokes.explanation: This is one of the best moments in the episode. Michael's guacamole confession is funny and devastating simultaneously — the image of Michael alone, working through enormous quantities of party guacamole after no-shows — is tragicomic perfection. 'I don't even know why I make it in such great quantities' implies he keeps making the same mistake, optimistic every time. This is The Office at its best: comedy that aches. Very high character integration — this is the Michael Scott experience distilled.

jokes.text: Michael talking head: 'I have an enormous amount of trouble trying to get people to come to my place. And I hate it. I can't tell you how much leftover guacamole I have ended up eating over the years. I don't even know why I make it in such great quantities.'
jokes.setup: Michael connects to Kelly's party abandonment through his own experience of people not showing up
jokes.punchline: The guacamole specificity — 'such great quantities' — transforms a sympathetic moment into an absurd one; Michael's personal tragedy is expressed in dip volume
jokes.explanation: One of the best Michael moments in the episode. The guacamole bit works on multiple levels: it's genuinely sympathetic (Michael making food for parties no one attends), absurd (the 'great quantities' detail), and ends with perfect self-unawareness ('I don't even know why I make it in such great quantities'). The combination of pathos and absurdity is exactly what The Office does best. Very high character integration — this is quintessential Michael Scott. Stands as a top-3 moment in the episode.

jokes.text: Michael tells Kelly: 'Here's what we're gonna do. We are going to sit here for a while, make it look good. And maybe you should cry. Can you make yourself cry?' Kelly: 'No problem.'
jokes.setup: Michael needs to make it look like Kelly is being disciplined without actually firing her
jokes.punchline: He stage-manages her fake crying — 'make it look good' — and Kelly's instant 'No problem' implies she has this skill readily available
jokes.explanation: Kelly's 'No problem' for on-demand crying is perfect — it confirms she has this talent in reserve, which is very Kelly. Michael stage-managing disciplinary optics is very Michael. The two characters' abilities combining here is genuinely funny.

jokes.text: Alex appears in New York to kidnap Pam for free wine and cheese at a Chuck Close retrospective — Pam: 'That's gonna be great. Who's Chuck Close?' then immediately: 'I love Chuck Close and his photo-realist paintings.'
jokes.setup: Pam is invited to a free art event; she asks 'Who's Chuck Close?' suggesting she doesn't know
jokes.punchline: Pam immediately pivots to 'I love Chuck Close and his photo-realist paintings' — suggesting she was correcting herself for Jim's benefit (he's in her ear)
jokes.explanation: The joke requires understanding the Bluetooth — Pam's sudden expertise on Chuck Close is for Jim's ears. She doesn't want Jim to know she doesn't know the artist she's going to see with another man. The Bluetooth premise creates a new comedic layer in the Pam/Alex scenes.

jokes.text: Jim via Bluetooth: 'That's it, I want to talk to this guy. Put me in his ear.'
jokes.setup: Jim is listening to Pam and Alex's conversation through the earpiece
jokes.punchline: Jim wants to be patched into Alex's ear — as if this is a spy operation — to interrogate him directly
jokes.explanation: Jim's jealousy expressed as a tactical surveillance request — 'put me in his ear' — is a funny application of the Bluetooth premise. The spy-operation framing of romantic jealousy is character-specific to this season's Jim/Pam setup.

jokes.text: Jim: 'I'm gonna make a bigger leap here. He is into you.' (about Alex, to Pam via Bluetooth)
jokes.setup: Jim is listening to Alex encourage Pam to stay in New York
jokes.punchline: Jim cuts to the chase — 'He is into you' — delivered with the dry certainty of a man who recognizes his own moves
jokes.explanation: Jim calling Alex's motivations accurately (he probably is into Pam) while being helpless to intervene is a nice tension note. The economy of 'He is into you' is good. Slightly undercut by not being fully paid off.

jokes.text: Dwight spots Jim's earpiece: 'Is that the Matsuhashi B400? World's tiniest bluetooth.' Jim: 'May I?' Dwight: 'Don't.'
jokes.setup: Dwight has been unaware of Jim's earpiece all day; he finally notices it
jokes.punchline: Dwight knows the exact model name by sight — 'Matsuhashi B400' — but Jim shuts down any further engagement with a flat 'Don't.'
jokes.explanation: The callback pays off — Dwight has been calling Jim a loser for talking to himself all day, and now he discovers the earpiece. His immediate tech-cataloguing ('Matsuhashi B400') is perfect Dwight. Jim's 'Don't.' is the funniest possible response — it ends the scene before Dwight can process the implications.

jokes.text: Dwight launches into the Schrute Farms wedding sales pitch with full professionalism: 'Congratulations on choosing Schrute Farms...' Michael: 'We haven't decided on anything yet.'
jokes.setup: Michael and Angela are considering Schrute Farms as a wedding venue — still undecided
jokes.punchline: Dwight opens with 'Congratulations on choosing Schrute Farms' — pre-deciding their decision — Michael has to correct him
jokes.explanation: Dwight assuming the sale before it's made is reliable character comedy — he's the worst kind of salesperson, simultaneously confident and presumptuous. Decent but not exceptional.

jokes.text: Michael says 'Deal!' before hearing the price; Dwight: 'You already said deal.' Angela: 'Pay him whatever he wants.' Michael: 'Can't argue with that.'
jokes.setup: Dwight is about to discuss pricing for the Schrute Farms wedding package
jokes.punchline: Michael says 'Deal' before the price is mentioned; when asked about price, Angela says 'Pay him whatever he wants' — both Michael and Angela are terrible negotiators
jokes.explanation: Michael's eagerness undermining his negotiating position is funny; Angela's 'Pay him whatever he wants' in her clipped authoritative voice is the funnier beat. Dwight barely concealing delight at this turn of events is the visual cap.

tmdb_overview: Dwight and Jim are shocked when they get the results of the annual customer survey report. Pam and Jim decide they want to spend every minute together using their bluetooth phones. Meanwhile, Angela and Andy pick an unusual location for their wedding.
